text_blocks.snippet: Fluid volume excess, also known as hypervolemia, is a condition where there's too much fluid in the body, primarily in the extracellular fluid (ECF) space. This can lead to symptoms like swelling (edema), weight gain, and even more serious complications like heart failure.
snippet_highlighted_words: a condition where there's too much fluid in the body, primarily in the extracellular fluid (ECF) space

text_blocks.snippet: Several factors can contribute to fluid volume excess, including:

list.snippet: Heart failure: When the heart can't pump blood effectively, fluid can back up and accumulate in the body.
Kidney failure: Impaired kidney function can lead to the body retaining excess sodium and water.
Cirrhosis: Liver disease can cause fluid to build up in the abdomen (ascites) and elsewhere.
Nephrotic syndrome: This kidney disorder can lead to protein loss in the urine, causing fluid retention.
IV fluids: Excessive administration of intravenous fluids can lead to volume overload.
High sodium intake: Consuming too much salt can lead to the body retaining more water.
Certain medications: Some medications can cause fluid retention as a side effect.

text_blocks.snippet: What are the symptoms of fluid volume excess?
Symptoms can vary depending on the severity and location of the fluid buildup, but may include:

list.snippet: Swelling (edema): This can occur in the feet, ankles, legs, hands, or face.
Weight gain: A sudden increase in weight can be a sign of fluid retention.
Shortness of breath: Fluid buildup in the lungs (pulmonary edema) can make it difficult to breathe.
Increased blood pressure: Excess fluid can put extra strain on the heart and blood vessels, leading to hypertension.
Bounding pulse: A strong, forceful heartbeat may be noticeable.
Distended neck veins: The veins in the neck may appear swollen and prominent.
Rapid heart rate (tachycardia): The heart may beat faster to compensate for the increased fluid volume.
Abdominal swelling (ascites): In severe cases, fluid can accumulate in the abdomen, causing it to appear distended.
Fatigue and weakness: Fluid volume excess can make you feel tired and weak.

text_blocks.snippet: How is fluid volume excess treated?
Treatment for fluid volume excess focuses on:

list.title: Removing excess fluid:
list.snippet: Diuretics (water pills) can help the kidneys remove excess fluid and sodium. In severe cases, dialysis may be necessary to remove fluid.

list.title: Addressing the underlying cause:
list.snippet: Treating the underlying condition, such as heart failure or kidney disease, is crucial for long-term management.

list.title: Restricting fluid and sodium intake:
list.snippet: Limiting the amount of fluids and sodium consumed can help prevent further fluid buildup.

list.title: Monitoring:
list.snippet: Regularly monitoring weight, intake and output (I&O), and vital signs (like blood pressure and heart rate) is important.
